note: Core fit, with the one miss falling in the favourable direction. MATCHES: 'successful' — owns or runs a business with operations across the UK, Europe and South Africa and employs a substantial team; he even articulates the ICP's own logic back at the rep ('if you can't look after yourself, how are you going to look after my business?'). 'Income' — stated without hedging when asked directly: '6k is within my budget', reinforced by 'Even if it was two grand, I think that's not the point'. 'Good_to_great' — the purest example of this criterion in the batch: 'I don't think I'm that far from my goals', wanting a six-pack in his forties and hip mobility, not rescue. 'Not_deconditioned' — trains every single day across weights, boxing and cycling, and leg presses 300 kg. MISS: 'neglected_health' — and this is the interesting one. The criterion says health should be the neglected area. For this prospect health is the MOST attended area of his life; he has trained consistently for twenty years, sleeps seven hours, meditates daily and eats a protein-rich diet. He fails the criterion by being too healthy, not by being in crisis. Scored 'core' because he satisfies the ICP's evident intent — a successful, affluent, already-capable man buying an upgrade — while exposing that 'neglected health' is written for a buyer who has let things slide, and does not describe the highly disciplined optimizer who is arguably the better customer. Worth logging alongside the Eddy assessment from the same day: both are core-fit optimizers, both confirmed the price was affordable, and neither bought on the call. If that pattern holds, the constraint on core-ICP conversion is not qualification, it is that this segment has no urgency and the process currently manufactures none for them.
